reference.source: Smith & Tanagho's General Urology / Campbell-Walsh Urology
clinicalPearls: Phimosis is an inability to retract the foreskin over the glans; it is physiological in most infants and young boys and usually resolves as natural preputial separation occurs with age

Pathological (acquired) phimosis follows scarring from recurrent balanitis, forced retraction, or the skin condition balanitis xerotica obliterans (lichen sclerosus), producing a firm white cicatricial ring
It must be distinguished from paraphimosis, in which a retracted foreskin becomes trapped behind the glans and cannot be reduced, causing painful swelling and constituting an emergency
Symptoms may include ballooning of the foreskin on voiding, difficulty with hygiene, recurrent infection, painful erections, and, in severe cases, obstructive voiding
Physiological phimosis is managed conservatively with reassurance, gentle hygiene, and avoidance of forcible retraction, often supplemented by topical corticosteroid application to soften the ring
Balanitis xerotica obliterans is an important pathological cause that typically requires circumcision and histological confirmation, and can involve the meatus and urethra
Circumcision or preputioplasty is indicated for true pathological phimosis, recurrent balanoposthitis, or troublesome symptoms not responding to conservative measures
Persistent phimosis in adults, particularly with lichen sclerosus, is a risk factor for penile carcinoma and warrants careful examination of the glans
reference.pathophysiology: In physiological phimosis the foreskin is non-retractile simply because natural adhesions between the inner prepuce and glans have not yet separated and the preputial opening is developmentally narrow. Pathological phimosis results from fibrosis and scarring of the preputial ring, most often due to chronic or recurrent inflammation (balanoposthitis), repeated trauma from forced retraction, or lichen sclerosus (balanitis xerotica obliterans), an inflammatory dermatosis that causes progressive sclerosis. The scarred, inelastic ring restricts retraction and may obstruct the urinary stream.
additionalInvestigations: Clinical examination of the foreskin, glans, and meatus
Assessment for the cicatricial white ring of lichen sclerosus
Urinalysis if infection or voiding symptoms are present
Histological examination of excised preputial tissue after circumcision, particularly when lichen sclerosus or malignancy is suspected
redFlags: Paraphimosis with a trapped, swollen, painful glans requiring emergency reduction
Severe phimosis causing obstructed voiding or acute urinary retention
Suspicious glans lesion or induration suggesting penile carcinoma
Features of lichen sclerosus with meatal or urethral involvement
reference.prognosis: Physiological phimosis almost always resolves with growth and conservative care; pathological phimosis is effectively cured by circumcision, but lichen sclerosus can recur or involve the meatus and carries a long-term association with penile malignancy.
pitfalls: Forcibly retracting a young boy's physiological phimosis, which can cause scarring and true phimosis
Mislabelling normal developmental non-retractility as pathological and recommending unnecessary surgery
Missing lichen sclerosus or an underlying penile malignancy in an adult with acquired phimosis
Confusing phimosis with paraphimosis and delaying emergency reduction
Overlooking meatal stenosis in patients with lichen sclerosus after circumcision
